¶
{{smaller block|The ''alonely'' rule of the land rested in the queen.
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chron., an. 1328.}}}}

¶
'''aloneness''' (ạ-lōn′nes), ''n.'' The state of being alone or without company.
{{smaller block|Watching over his ''aloneness.''
{{right|''J. Legge'', Life of Confucius, p. 44.}}}}

'''along<sup>1</sup>''' (ạ-lông′), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [< ME. ''along'', ''olong'', earlier ''anlong'', also (by confusion with the early forms of ''endlong'', q. v.) ''andelong'', ''endelong'', ''endlang'', etc., < AS. ''andlang'', along (= OFries. ''ondling'', ''ondlinga'', ''ondlenge'' = G. ''entlang'', along), < ''and-'', over against, away toward, + ''lang'', long: see ''and-'', ''a-''<sup>5</sup>, and ''long''<sup>1</sup>. Orig. (in AS.) an adj., ‘stretching long or far away,’ applied, as found, only to periods of time, ‘the livelong’ day or night, but prob. also to space; then used adverbially with dependent gen., afterward taken as direct obj. of ''along'' as a prep., the prep. implied in the orig. gen. being subsequently expressed by ''on'', ''upon'', ''by'', ''with'', thus giving ''along'' the construction of an adv. Quite different from ''along''<sup>2</sup>, owing to, q. v.] '''I.''' ''prep.'' Through or by the length of; from one end to or toward the other of; lengthwise or in a longitudinal direction through, over, or by the side of: implying motion or direction: as, to walk ''along'' a river or highway.
{{smaller block|And the messages that go ''along'' my nerves do not consist in any continuous action.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, I. 258.}}}}

'''II.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' By the length; lengthwise; parallel to or in a line with the length.
{{smaller block|<poem>Some laid ''along'',
And bound with burning wires, on spokes of wheels are hung.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''alongshore''' (a̤-lông′shōr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''along''<sup>1</sup> + ''shore''<sup>1</sup>.] By the shore or coast; lengthwise of the shore and near it.
{{smaller block|I see . . . California quartz-mountains dumped down in New York to be repiled architecturally ''along-shore'' from Canada to Cuba, and thence westward to California again.
{{right|''Emerson'', Civilization.}}}}

'''alongshoreman''' (a̤-lông′shōr-man), ''n.''; pl. ''alongshoremen'' (-men). [< ''alongshore'' + ''man.''] A laborer employed about docks or wharves and in the loading and unloading of vessels. Commonly shortened to ’''longshoreman.''

'''alongside''' (a̤-lông′sīd), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ''along''<sup>1</sup> + ''side''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''adv.'' Along or by the side; at or to the side of anything, as a ship: as, to be ''alongside'' of the wall.
{{smaller block|Several large boats came ''alongside.''
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 18.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' Beside; by the side of: as, the vessel lay ''alongside'' the wharf.
{{smaller block|We first tested this case by laying it ''alongside'' the historic facts in the case.
{{right|''S. Lanier'', The English Novel, p. 46.}}}}

'''alongst†''' (a̤-lôngst′), ''prep.'' [ME. ''alongest, in longes''; < ''along''<sup>1</sup> + ''-est, -st,'' after ''amongst'' from ''among, against'' from ''again,'' etc.] Along; through or by the length of.
{{smaller block|The Turks did keep straight watch and ward in all their parts ''alongst'' the sea-coast.
{{right|''Knolles'', Hist. Turks.}}}}

''areatus'', having areas or spots), a disease of the hairy regions of the skin, characterized by the appearance of one or more bald spots, extending themselves with rounding outlines, and sometimes by coalescence producing complete baldness. The bald spot has a center which is naked and smooth, surrounded by a peripheral zone, scaly and presenting numerous broken short hairs. It is by some considered due to a vegetable parasite, and by others to nervous disturbance. Also called ''area Celsi'', or simply ''area''.—'''Alopecia pityrodes''' (NL. ''pityrodes'', bran-like), a disease of the hairy parts of the skin, characterized by a progressive reduction in the length, size, and number of the hairs, attended with an abundant furfuraceous accumulation on the surface of the skin.—'''Alopecia unguium''' (L. ''unguis'', a nail), falling off of the nails.}}

¶'''alopecian''' (al-ō-pē′si-an), ''n.'' A shark of the family ''Alopeciidæ''. ''Sir J. Richardson.''

'''Alopecias''' (al-ọ̄-pē′si-as), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀλωπεκίας, the thresher-shark, < ἀλώπηξ, a fox, also a kind of shark.] Same as ''Alopias''.

'''alopeciid''' (al-ọ̄-pē′si-id), ''n.'' A fox-shark; a shark of the family ''Alopeciidæ''.

'''Alopeciidæ''' (al-ọ̄-pē-sī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Alopecias'' + ''-idæ''.] Same as ''Alopiidæ''.

'''alopecist''' (al′ọ̄-pe-sist), ''n.'' [< ''alopecia'' + ''-ist''.] One who undertakes to cure or prevent baldness. ''N. E. D.''

'''alopecoid''' (al-ō-pē′koid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< Gr. *ἀλωπεκοειδής, contr. ἀλωπεκώδης, fox-like, < ἀλώπηξ, fox, + εἶδος, form.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Fox-like; vulpine: applied to a group or series of carnivorous mammals of which the common fox is the type, as distinguished from the thoöid series, which includes the dogs and wolves.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''Alopiidæ''' (al-ō-pī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., shortened from ''Alopeciidæ''; also written ''Alopiadæ''; < ''Alopias'' + ''-idæ'', ''-adæ''.] A family of anarthrous selachians, represented by the genus ''Alopias''.

'''Alosa''' (a-lō′sä), ''n.'' [L., also ''alausa'', > F. ''alose'', > E. ''allice'', q. v.] A genus of fishes, of the family ''Clupeidæ'', including the shad (which see). Also written ''Alausa''.

'''alose<sup>1</sup>''' (a-lōs′), ''n.'' A member of the genus ''Alosa''.

'''alose<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [< OF. ''aloser'', < ''a-'' + ''los'', praise: see ''a-''<sup>11</sup> and ''lose''<sup>2</sup>.] To praise. ''Chaucer.''

'''alouate, alouatte''' (al′ö-at), ''n.'' [Prob. a F. form of a native name.] A name given by French naturalists, as Buffon, to the red howling monkey of Guiana, afterward known as ''Mycetes seniculus'' (Illiger); hence used as a general name, like ''hurleur'', for the South American howlers. See cut under ''howler''.

'''alouatta''' (al-ö-at′ä), ''n.'' Same as ''alouate''.

'''alouchi, aluchi''' (ä-lö′chi), ''n.'' [Native name.] A resin obtained from ''Icica heterophylla'', a tree of Madagascar. It is thought to have some medicinal properties. See ''acouchi-resin''.

'''aloud''' (a-loud′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [ME. ''aloud'', ''a loude''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''loud''. Cf. ''alow''<sup>1</sup>, ''ahigh''.] '''1.''' With a loud voice or great noise; loudly.
{{smaller block|Cry ''aloud'', spare not.
{{right|Is. lviii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Audibly; with the natural tone of the voice as distinguished from whispering: as, he has a severe cold and can hardly speak ''aloud''.

'''à l’outrance''' (ä lö-troṅs′). See ''à outrance''.

'''alow<sup>1</sup>''' (a-lō′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [ME. ''alow'', ''alowe'', ''alough'', ''alogh'', ''aloȝ''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''low''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''be-''

She is ''alone.''{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|I am ''alone'' the villain of the earth.{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 6.}}}} '''4†.''' Devoid; destitute. {{smaller block|For bothe a wydowe was she and ''allone'' Of ony frend to whom she dorst hire mone.{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 98.}}}} '''To let alone.''' {{smaller|See ''let.'' ='''Syn.''' ''Alone, Only.'' The attributive use of ''alone'' is now very rare. In the Bible and earlier English ''alone'' is often used for the adverb ''only'', but it is now becoming restricted to its own sense of solitary, unaccompanied by other persons or things.}} {{smaller block|Who can forgive sins but God ''alone?''{{right|Luke v. 21.}}}} {{smaller block|Not ''alone'' at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia.{{right|Acts xix. 26.}}}} {{smaller block|In each of these examples ''only'' would now be considered better, though ''not alone'' for ''not only'' is in common use. ''Alone'' means unaccompanied: as, he stood ''alone.'' ''Only'' applies to that of which there is no other: as, an ''only'' son; adverbially, ''only'' this.}} {{smaller block|And I ''only'' am escaped ''alone'' to tell thee.{{right|Job i. 15.}}}} '''alonely†''' (a̤-lōn′li), ''adv.'' and ''a.''  [< ME.
